findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add `src/rebar/_cli/_init.py` to the Files section and enumerate `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` (init.py:628) as a co-edit target, since it uses the same broken local-tracking-ref predicate and gates the auto-init path that must reach the new fail-closed logic in `_mount_or_create_branch`.
evidence: init.py:646-648: `return _git_ok(repo, 'rev-parse', '--verify', branch) or _git_ok(repo, 'rev-parse', '--verify', f'{remote_name}/{branch}')` — same local-tracking-ref predicate as the buggy path

Plan Approach: 'Before orphan-bootstrapping, probe the configured remote' — but pending_init_attaches_to_existing is also called before init runs (it decides WHETHER init runs), and uses the same broken local predicate
_cli/_init.py:100: `if _init_cmd.pending_init_attaches_to_existing(repo_root):` — used as the gate for non-interactive attach
_cli/_init.py:237: `if _init_cmd.pending_init_is_symlink(root) or _init_cmd.pending_init_attaches_to_existing(root):` — used in the auto-mount path
Plan Files section names only `src/rebar/_commands/init.py, tests` — `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` and its callers in `_cli/_init.py` are absent
findings.finding: `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` (init.py:628) contains the identical broken predicate (`rev-parse --verify origin/tickets` on the local tracking ref) and is NOT named as an edit target, yet it gates the same auto-init path described in the plan. Fixing only `_mount_or_create_branch` leaves the consent gate consulting stale local state, which can cause the auto-init path to either incorrectly skip the new probe (returning False when the remote has tickets but the local tracking ref is absent) or, after the fix, produce inconsistent behavior between the gate and the mount logic.
scenarios: Fresh clone where `origin/tickets` exists but the local tracking ref `origin/tickets` is absent (the exact P1 scenario): the new remote probe in `_mount_or_create_branch` fails closed correctly, but `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` still returns False, so `_cli/_init.py:100` never even calls `init_core` — the non-interactive path exits with 'requires an interactive terminal' instead of the new 'cannot reach remote' error.

If `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` is updated to call the new remote probe (making it return True), the consent gate correctly triggers `init_core`, which then runs the bounded probe and fails closed — that is the intended flow, but neither the gate update nor `_cli/_init.py` are named as edit targets.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Files section, add `src/rebar/_cli/_init.py` alongside `src/rebar/_commands/init.py`. In the Approach, note that `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` must be updated to call (or delegate to) the same remote probe, so that the consent gate and the mount logic agree on whether `origin/tickets` exists.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend the plan's scope to also update `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` (init.py:628-648) — which uses the same local-ref predicate as the orphan-bootstrap path — to use the bounded remote probe so both the consent gate and the mount path share a single, consistent discriminator.
evidence: Ticket comment: 'The same purely-local predicate backed the auto-init consent gate (init.py:645), which is why the reporter's FIRST command died with auto-init requires an interactive terminal.'
init.py:646-648: `return _git_ok(repo, 'rev-parse', '--verify', branch) or _git_ok(repo, 'rev-parse', '--verify', f'{remote_name}/{branch}')` — same local-ref check as the mount path
Plan Approach section: 'Before orphan-bootstrapping, probe the configured remote.' — scopes only to the bootstrap path, silent on the consent gate.
ABSENCE: no mention of `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` anywhere in the plan text
findings.finding: The plan's fix targets only `_mount_or_create_branch` (init.py:366-382) but the confirmed root cause also affects `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` (init.py:628-648), which uses the identical local-ref predicate (`rev-parse --verify {remote_name}/{branch}`) as the auto-init consent gate. The ticket's own root-cause comment explicitly names this dual-predicate problem. Without updating `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` to use the remote probe, the consent gate will still misclassify a 'remote has tickets but local tracking ref is absent' situation as 'no existing store', allowing auto-init to proceed into the orphan-bootstrap path — the very failure mode the plan aims to close.
scenarios: Auto-init in a narrow clone (single-branch, no tracking ref for 'tickets'): `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` returns False, auto-init is blocked (requires TTY) or proceeds unchecked into _mount_or_create_branch which, even after the plan's fix, still may behave unexpectedly if the consent gate made the wrong call.

The exact P1 scenario (tracking ref absent, remote has 49k-commit tickets branch): `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` returns False, auto-init gate does not classify this as a 'safe attach', and the fixed orphan-bootstrap guard alone does not protect headless/auto-init callers.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a shared helper (e.g., `_probe_remote_branch(repo, remote_name, branch, timeout)`) that runs `git ls-remote --exit-code <remote> refs/heads/<branch>` with a timeout, returning `remote | unreachable | none`. Have both `_mount_or_create_branch` and `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` call it; this matches the architectural fix described in the ticket comment ('one shared discriminator ... used by BOTH the mount path and the consent gate').

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how the bounded ls-remote probe is implemented given that `run_git_write` (used by `_git()` in `init.py`) has no `timeout` parameter — either add a timeout-capable helper or call `run_git` directly, matching the pattern in `_ref_lock.py`.
evidence: Plan: 'Keep the probe bounded so an unreachable remote does not hang init.'
`init.py:86-87`: `_git()` calls `run_git_write(cwd, *args, check=False)` with no timeout forwarding.
`gitutil.py:239-267`: `run_git_write` signature is `(tracker, *args, check=False)` — no timeout parameter.
`_ref_lock.py:315`: the same `ls-remote` probe in the reconciler passes `timeout=_REMOTE_TIMEOUT_SECS` directly to `run_git`, bypassing `run_git_write`.
Evidence class: Contradicted — the helper's published signature confirms it cannot forward a timeout.
findings.finding: The plan requires a bounded `git ls-remote` probe inside `init.py`, but the existing `_git()` / `_git_ok()` helpers route through `run_git_write`, whose public signature accepts no `timeout` argument — making a bounded call impossible through those helpers without modification.
scenarios: The new probe is wired through `_git()` → `run_git_write()` without adding a timeout; the 'bounded' guarantee is silently lost and an unreachable remote hangs init just as the original fetch did.
The author adds a raw `subprocess.run` call inline but this diverges from the repo's established abstraction pattern, risking the index-lock retry logic being skipped for a write op.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a thin `_git_remote(cwd, timeout, *args)` helper in `init.py` that calls `run_git(cwd, *args, timeout=timeout, check=False)` directly (as `_ref_lock.py` already does), and use it exclusively for the ls-remote probe. Keep `_git()` / `_git_ok()` for local ops.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the blackhole mechanism for the unreachable-remote AC test (e.g., a loopback TCP listener that accepts but never responds, or `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` override), so the test actually exercises the timeout path rather than fast-failing via ECONNREFUSED/NXDOMAIN.
evidence: Plan AC: 'With an **unreachable** remote, init fails within a bounded time rather than hanging. Tier: **CLI subprocess** against a blackholed endpoint.'
No existing test in `tests/` uses a stalling TCP socket or network-level blackhole (search for 'blackhole' returned no results).
Existing unreachable-remote tests in `tests/integration/test_concurrency_regression.py:494-495` use a non-existent path (`does-not-exist.git`), which produces an instant error — not a hang.
Evidence class: Unverified — no established fixture for a stalling-socket blackhole exists in the test suite.
findings.finding: The AC for the 'unreachable remote' test tier specifies 'CLI subprocess against a blackholed endpoint' but the plan does not describe how the blackhole is constructed in tests; a naive non-existent hostname may fail fast (NXDOMAIN) rather than stall, making the bound-checking test vacuously pass without exercising the timeout path.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — third bullet ('With an unreachable remote, init fails within a bounded time')
scenarios: Test uses a non-routable IP that fails fast with ECONNREFUSED, so the 15-second bound is never actually tested.
Test uses a hostname that resolves but stalls at TCP-connect, which requires a listening-but-silent server that must be set up and torn down in the test fixture.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the probe's error-handling policy for unexpected failures (auth errors, unexpected exit codes, unparseable output): should they all fail closed (non-zero exit) or produce a distinct error, and add an AC covering at least one such case.
evidence: Plan specifies three cases: (1) reachable+advertises → refuse, (2) no such branch → bootstrap, (3) unreachable → bounded fail. It is silent on: auth error, unexpected git exit code, malformed ls-remote output, or partial connectivity.
Absence: no 'else/unknown error → fail closed' branch is described.
findings.finding: The probe's failure modes beyond timeout and 'branch absent' are unspecified: if the remote-probe command (e.g., `git ls-remote`) exits with an unexpected error (auth failure, DNS partial resolution, malformed output), the plan does not state whether init should fail closed, fail open, or surface a distinct error — leaving an ambiguous partial-state path.
findings.location: Approach section: 'probe the configured remote. If it is reachable and advertises the configured tickets branch, refuse to bootstrap'
scenarios: SSH key not configured: `git ls-remote` exits non-zero with 'Permission denied' — neither 'unreachable' nor 'branch absent'; plan doesn't specify behavior.
Proxy returns garbage: ls-remote output is unparseable — could silently fall through to bootstrap if the parser treats it as 'no branch found'.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a default 'fail closed on any probe error other than confirmed branch-absent' rule to the Approach section, and add a brief AC: 'Any unexpected probe error (e.g., auth failure) also fails non-zero and does not bootstrap.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC (and specify the approach) for the probe-error third state — when the remote probe itself fails with a transport/auth error (exit non-zero for a reason other than 'branch not found'), document whether init should fail closed or bootstrap, and add a CLI subprocess test for this case.
evidence: Plan approach: 'If it is reachable AND advertises the configured tickets branch, refuse to bootstrap. Only bootstrap when the remote genuinely has no such branch'
This binary framing (reachable+found | no branch) omits a third state: probe returned an error (auth failure, transport error, partial connectivity)
AC#3 covers unreachable remote (bounded failure), but not a reachable remote where the probe command exits with a transport/auth error rather than a clean branch-list result
ABSENCE: no AC verifies what happens when `git ls-remote` exits non-zero due to auth/transport error vs. simply returning no matching branch
findings.finding: The plan's approach describes a binary probe outcome (reachable-and-advertises-branch vs. genuinely-no-branch) but does not specify the behavior when the probe itself encounters an error state — e.g., an authentication failure, a partial-connectivity error, or a git transport error that is neither 'remote reachable and branch found' nor 'clean unreachable'. Without a specified and tested behavior for this third state, the implementation may inadvertently treat a probe error as 'no such branch' and silently proceed with orphan-bootstrap, reproducing the original P1 defect under a different trigger.
findings.location: Approach section + Acceptance Criteria (no AC covers probe-error third state)
scenarios: A rebar user in a corporate environment with git-over-SSH where the agent key lacks permission: probe fails with auth error, init silently orphan-bootstraps, reproducing P1 01e8-302b under a different trigger
CI pipeline where the remote is reachable but rate-limited: probe returns a transport error, init treats it as 'no branch', bootstraps orphan
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit AC: 'When the remote probe exits non-zero for a reason other than an empty branch list (e.g., auth failure, transport error), init fails closed with a non-zero exit and an informative error message.' In the Approach section, clarify: treat any probe error that is not a clean empty-branch-list as a failure-closed condition, not as a legitimate first-init trigger.

evidence: 1 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Explicitly state in the Approach section that an unreachable remote (probe timeout or connection failure) MUST exit non-zero, not fall through to bootstrap, to resolve the contradiction with AC3.
evidence: Approach: 'Only bootstrap when the remote genuinely has no such branch (the legitimate first-init case)'
Approach: 'Keep the probe bounded so an unreachable remote does not hang init' — says 'bounded' but not 'fail'
AC3: 'With an unreachable remote, init fails within a bounded time rather than hanging'
An implementer reading only the Approach could infer: unreachable → unknown → fall through to bootstrap, contradicting AC3
findings.finding: The Approach section describes only two explicit disposition cases for the probe (reachable+advertises-branch → refuse; remote has no branch → bootstrap) but omits what happens when the remote is unreachable — leaving the implementer free to infer 'fall through to bootstrap,' which directly contradicts AC3's assertion that init 'fails within a bounded time' on an unreachable remote.
scenarios: Implementer reads Approach, implements unreachable-remote as silent-bootstrap (since remote 'genuinely has no known branch'), re-introducing the P1 bug for the network-partition case.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the Approach: 'If the remote is unreachable (probe times out or connection is refused), treat this as an indeterminate state and exit non-zero with a message indicating the remote could not be reached; do not bootstrap.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm whether the plan intends to reuse `_remote_ref_absent()` from `_ref_lock.py` (or an equivalent shared helper in `_store/`) for the remote probe, rather than re-implementing `git ls-remote --exit-code` exit-code discrimination and timeout inline in `init.py`.
evidence: Plan: 'probe the configured remote. If it is reachable and advertises the configured tickets branch, refuse to bootstrap … Keep the probe bounded so an unreachable remote does not hang init.'

`_remote_ref_absent()` at `_ref_lock.py:301-330` performs exactly this: `git ls-remote --exit-code` bounded by `_REMOTE_TIMEOUT_SECS=30.0`, returns `False` (present), `True` (absent), `None` (unreachable/transport error).
The plan names only `src/rebar/_commands/init.py` in its Files section, with no reference to the existing probe utility.
findings.finding: The plan's 'bounded remote probe' is already implemented in the codebase as `_remote_ref_absent()` in `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/_ref_lock.py` (line 301–330), which uses `git ls-remote --exit-code` with a `_REMOTE_TIMEOUT_SECS=30.0` bound and the correct three-way exit-code discrimination (0=present, 2=absent, other=transport failure→None). The plan does not acknowledge this existing utility, creating a risk of NIH reimplementation inline in `init.py`.
scenarios: Implementer writes a second `ls-remote` wrapper in `init.py`, duplicating exit-code discrimination logic and timeout handling already in `_ref_lock.py`, leading to two divergent implementations of the same probe.
The new inline probe omits the three-way None/unknown case (unreachable → treat as 'no branch') and silently bootstraps an orphan when the remote is merely unreachable, recreating the original bug.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a note in the Files section or Approach: either (a) extract `_remote_ref_absent` (or a thin wrapper) to a shared location accessible from `init.py` and reuse it, or (b) explicitly document why a fresh inline implementation is preferred (e.g. the reconciler module is not importable from `init.py`). If the reconciler module is unavailable at init time, a one-liner `subprocess` call reproducing the three-way exit-code contract is still only ~8 lines — document that explicitly so the three-way discrimination (exit 0 / exit 2 / anything else) is not accidentally collapsed.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Before implementing a new remote-probe helper in `init.py`, consider reusing or extracting `_remote_ref_absent()` from `_ref_lock.py` (lines 301–330), which already provides the identical `git ls-remote --exit-code` contract (0=present, 2=absent, other=fail-closed) with a 30s timeout — or document why a separate implementation in init is preferred.
evidence: Plan Approach: 'probe the configured remote. If it is reachable and advertises the configured tickets branch, refuse to bootstrap'
_remote_ref_absent() at _ref_lock.py:301-330 implements git ls-remote --exit-code with identical semantics: exit 0 → present, exit 2 → absent, else → None (unknown/fail-closed)

findings.finding: The codebase already contains `_remote_ref_absent()` in `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/_ref_lock.py` (lines 301–330), which implements the exact `git ls-remote --exit-code` probe the plan re-invents for `init.py`: same exit-code discrimination (0=present, 2=absent, other=unreachable/fail-closed), same 30s timeout bound, same locale-independence rationale. The plan commits to building a new probe without considering this existing utility.
scenarios: The plan author implements a second `ls-remote` probe in init.py with subtly different timeout or exit-code handling, creating two divergent implementations of the same semantic contract that can drift independently.
A future change to the ls-remote probe semantics (e.g., adding retry logic, changing the timeout) needs to be applied in two places.
findings.suggested_fix: Extract `_remote_ref_absent()` (and `_REMOTE_TIMEOUT_SECS`) from `_ref_lock.py` into a shared utility module (e.g., `rebar._store.gitutil` or a new `rebar._store.remote`), then import and call it from both `init.py` and `_ref_lock.py`. Alternatively, if coupling to `_ref_lock` internals is undesirable, import the function directly from `_ref_lock` in `init.py` with a comment noting the shared contract.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an explicit acknowledgment of the exit-behavior breaking change and a back-out plan (e.g., a flag to restore legacy behavior, or a documented rollback procedure) to satisfy T4's reversibility requirement.

scenarios: A CI pipeline calls `rebar init` and pipes into the next command unconditionally; after this change it starts failing builds where the remote is slow, with no documented back-out.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a message-content criterion for the unreachable-remote path (AC 3) — analogous to AC 4 — specifying that the error names the remote, indicates network/timeout cause, and provides a concrete remediation (e.g., 'check connectivity and retry').
evidence: AC 3: 'With an unreachable remote, init fails within a bounded time rather than hanging. Tier: CLI subprocess against a blackholed endpoint.'
AC 4: 'The error message names the remote, the branch, and a concrete remediation. Tier: unit on the message.'

AC 4 does not scope its message criterion to both the reachable-with-tickets and unreachable error paths; the unit test it implies covers only one error message variant, leaving the unreachable-remote UX path without a specified message contract.
findings.finding: AC 3 specifies that an unreachable remote causes init to 'fail within a bounded time' but neither AC 3 nor AC 4 specifies what the user-visible error message or remediation text should be in that case. AC 4's message spec (naming remote, branch, and remediation) is written against the reachable-but-advertises-tickets scenario. A user hitting a network outage during init will receive an unspecified error with no concrete next step.
scenarios: A developer runs `rebar init` from a laptop on a flaky VPN. The remote probe times out. Init exits non-zero (per AC 3) but the error text is unspecified — the user does not know whether the remote is unreachable, credentials failed, or the tickets branch exists on the remote and they should not retry with bootstrap flags.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend AC 4 to cover both error variants, or add an AC 4b: 'When the remote is unreachable, the error message identifies the remote, states that it could not be contacted within the timeout, and instructs the user to check connectivity and retry.'

metrics.claim_path: no-llm/no-network (structural; the fast claim check is a local HMAC verify)
